title: Factors, Multiples and Prime Numbers
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Factors, Multiples and Prime Numbers. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Factors, multiples and primes

A positive integer d is a factor of n when n/d is an integer; n is then a multiple of d. Factors occur in pairs: for 36, the pairs are (\(1,36\)), (\(2,18\)), (\(3,12\)), (\(4,9\)), and (\(6,6\)). A prime greater than 1 has exactly two positive factors; a composite number has more than two. One is neither.

Prime factorisation and divisor count

Write a number as a product of prime powers. If (\(N=p^a q^b r^c\)), each divisor chooses an exponent from 0 through the corresponding exponent, so the divisor count is (\((a+1)(b+1)(c+1)\)). The greatest common factor uses the smaller exponent of each common prime; the least common multiple uses the larger exponent of every prime present.

Worked example: (\(360=2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5\)) has (\((3+1)(2+1)(1+1)=24\)) positive divisors. For 36 and 60, the GCF is (\(2^2 \times 3=12\)), while the LCM is (\(2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5=180\)).

Perfect powers

A prime factorisation is a perfect square when every exponent is even, and a perfect cube when every exponent is divisible by 3. To make a number a square by multiplication, supply the missing prime factors needed to make all exponents even.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• To test n for primality, test prime divisors only up to the square root of n.
  • For divisor counts, factor first instead of listing divisors.
  • Compare prime exponents in columns for GCF and LCM.
  • For the smallest multiplier making a square or cube, balance exponent remainders.
  • For two positive integers, verify GCF times LCM equals their product.

Common errors

  • Do not count 1 as prime or composite.
  • An LCM includes primes occurring in either number, not only their common primes.
  • A perfect square has an odd divisor count because its square-root factor pairs with itself.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• If (\(N=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...\)), then (\(d(N)=\prod_i(a_i+1)\)).
  • GCF: minimum common exponents. LCM: maximum exponents.
  • Coprime positive integers have GCF 1 and LCM equal to their product.
  • Square: all prime exponents even. Cube: all exponents multiples of 3.
  • Trial division through the square root of n is enough to test primality.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    How many positive divisors does (\(360=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5\)) have?

    1. (\(12\))
    2. (\(18\))
    3. (\(24\))
    4. (\(30\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(24\))

    Use the divisor-count formula: (\((3+1)(2+1)(1+1)=4\cdot3\cdot2=24\)).

  2. Core:

    Which number is prime?

    1. (\(21\))
    2. (\(27\))
    3. (\(29\))
    4. (\(35\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(29\))

    The square root of 29 is less than 6. Test primes 2, 3 and 5: none divides 29, so 29 is prime.

  3. Foundation:

    Find the greatest common factor of (\(36\)) and (\(48\)).

    1. (\(6\))
    2. (\(8\))
    3. (\(12\))
    4. (\(16\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(12\))

    The common prime factors with minimum exponents are (\(2^2 \times 3=12\)).

  4. Standard:

    How many positive divisors does (\(2^4 \times 3^2\)) have?

    1. (\(8\))
    2. (\(12\))
    3. (\(15\))
    4. (\(18\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(15\))

    Apply the divisor formula: (\((4+1)(2+1)=5 \times 3=15\)).

  5. Challenge:

    What is the least positive integer that must multiply (\(180\)) to make a perfect square?

    1. (\(2\))
    2. (\(3\))
    3. (\(5\))
    4. (\(10\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(5\))

    (\(180=2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5\)). Only the exponent of 5 is odd, so multiply by 5; (\(900=30^2\)).
